query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A brief intermediate‐temperature annealing treatment applied to the as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve both room-temperature tensile ductility and strength by promoting interfacial homogenization and the formation of nanoscale precipitates at colony boundaries that suppress microcrack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation under tensile loading.
generation.intervention: A controlled annealing treatment at an intermediate temperature (for example, near 0.8–0.9 times the eutectic temperature) for a short duration (e.g., 30–60 minutes) followed by rapid cooling to room temperature.
generation.conditions: Annealing should be carried out in an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation. The applied temperature must be high enough to allow limited interfacial diffusion but low enough to avoid full coarsening or dissolution of the lamellar microstructure. Room-temperature tensile tests will be used for mechanical evaluation.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial bonding and the in-situ formation of nanoscale precipitates (or intermetallic particles) at the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment promotes modest diffusion at internal interfaces, which relieves stress concentrations and forms stabilizing interfacial precipitates that both impede crack nucleation and propagation and provide additional strengthening via a fine-scale dispersion effect. This dual effect cooperatively increases ductility without sacrificing strength relative to the brittle, as-cast lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the annealed alloy is predicted to exhibit higher yield strength and an increase in tensile ductility (improved elongation-to-failure) due to reduced microcrack initiation at internal boundaries while retaining the beneficial dual-phase architecture.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies, which typically shows high strength but limited tensile ductility due to microcrack formation along weak interphase boundaries.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective only if the annealing temperature and time are optimized to allow sufficient interfacial modification without causing excessive coarsening of the lamellar structure. This hypothesis applies for room-temperature tensile loading conditions and may not hold if tested under very high strain rates or temperatures where the modified interfaces could behave differently.
generation.uncertainty: The precise range of the annealing parameters and the resulting improvement magnitudes in strength and ductility are uncertain and will depend on the specific alloy composition and processing setup.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one retained in the as-cast state and another subjected to the specified intermediate-temperature annealing treatment. Perform microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM/SEM for interfacial precipitates and lamellar spacing) and conduct room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength and elongation.
measurements: Quantitative microstructural characterization (e.g., precipitate size, distribution, and lamellar spacing)
Tensile properties such as yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation-to-failure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show both an increase in yield strength and an improved elongation-to-failure (or show no statistically significant improvement relative to the as-cast baseline), then the hypothesis is rejected.
